# Online Psychic Reading vs In-Person

> Source: https://mysticdo.com/guides/online-psychic-vs-in-person

Comparison · Intent level 3
Same service, different machine. Online wins on price, choice, and accountability. In-person wins on rapport and immersion. The reader matters more than the channel — but the channel still changes what you get.

Updated: September 2026 · Reading time: ~5 min

### Direct answer

Choose **online** if you want lower cost, far more reader choice, written records, and platform refund protection — the right default for a first reading. Choose **in-person** if you already trust a specific local reader and value the ritual of a face-to-face session. Format changes the experience; it doesn't change the reader's skill. Validate the reader first, then pick the channel.

### Key takeaways

- **Online wins on mechanics**: 10–100× more reader choice, lower entry cost ($20–$60 vs $80–$200), refund policies, and chat transcripts you can reread.
- **In-person wins on experience**: undivided attention, physical presence, and the ritual weight some people need to take a session seriously.
- **Accountability is asymmetric** — online platforms publish refund policies and reviews; a local reader's accountability is their reputation in one town.
- **Neither format is inherently more accurate** — a generic reader is generic on video and across a table.
- **Default path**: test online cheaply → if you find a reader who fits, the channel stops mattering.

## The full comparison

Across the dimensions that actually change your outcome:

| Dimension | Online (platform: chat / phone / video) | In-person (local reader) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Best question type | Specific, focused questions; anything you'd rather not ask face-to-face | Bigger life-arc conversations where you want time and presence |
| Reader choice | Hundreds to thousands of readers, filterable by specialty and price | Whoever practices within driving distance — often a handful |
| Output form | Chat (written record), phone (voice), video (face) — chat and some calls are saved | Conversation across a table; you take your own notes |
| Personalization | High — and anonymity means you share more honestly | High — plus the reader picks up physical presence and energy |
| Typical price | $1–$15/min; intro offers common. First session $20–$60 | $60–$300 per session, usually 45–60 min, no intro pricing |
| Accountability | Published refund policies, platform reviews, support tickets | Word of mouth; refunds rare and informal |
| Best for | First readings, testing readers, specific questions, privacy, small budgets | People with a trusted local reader, or who need the ritual of presence |
| Limitations | Quality varies wildly inside platforms; per-minute drift; no physical rapport | Tiny selection, higher entry cost, no transcript, awkward to walk out early |

## What going online actually changes

Three structural shifts, one behavioral one:

- **Selection explodes.** Your town may have five readers. A large platform has five thousand, filterable by specialty, price, format, and rating. Selection is the single biggest quality lever in this market — and online is where it lives.
- **The cost floor collapses.** A local session starts around $60–$100 before you know if the reader fits. An online test session with an intro offer runs $20–$40. You can validate three readers online for the price of one local appointment.
- **Accountability appears.** Platforms publish refund windows, keep review histories the reader can't delete, and process complaints. None of that exists across a kitchen table.
- **And the behavioral shift: honesty gets easier.** Many people describe their real situation — the affair, the no-contact ex, the money fear — more candidly to a stranger in a chat window than to a face across a table. Better input, better reading.

## What in-person still does better

In-person isn't obsolete — it's narrower. It wins when:

- **You already have the reader.** A local reader you've tested and trust beats an anonymous platform roster. Relationship continuity is the one thing platforms can't productize.
- **The ritual is part of the point.** For some people, sitting in a quiet room with cards and a person's full attention is what makes them take the session seriously enough to act on it. If that's you, a chat window will feel thin — and the reading will land thinner.
- **The session is the event.** A milestone reading — a major life decision, a grief session — sometimes deserves an hour of undivided presence rather than a metered per-minute clock.

The format risks invert too: walking out of a bad in-person session at minute ten is socially painful, so people sit through it — and pay for all of it. Online, ending early is two clicks and often refunded.

## Cost reality check

**Pricing snapshot — checked September 2026.** Ranges reflect publicly listed prices across major platforms and independent readers; per-provider sources will be linked as provider reviews publish. [How we track pricing](https://mysticdo.com/methodology#research).

| What you're testing | Online cost | In-person cost |
| --- | --- | --- |
| “Is this reader any good?” (first session) | $20–$60 with intro offer, end-able early, often refundable | $60–$150, paid in full whether it lands or not |
| “A serious session on a real decision” | $50–$150 for 30–60 focused minutes | $100–$300 for a structured hour |
| “Ongoing guidance over months” | Per-minute drift risk — needs discipline; can reach $100s/mo | Fixed session pricing — predictable, but each session is a trip |

For the full price mechanics — per-minute vs per-session, intro offers, drift — see [How Much Does a Psychic Reading Cost?](https://mysticdo.com/guides/psychic-reading-cost)

## Real situations — which channel

### Go online when…

- “I've never had a reading and want to test the format without committing $150.” → Platform, intro offer, 15 minutes, one question.
- “My question is private — I'd never say it out loud to someone in my town.” → Chat or phone; anonymity is a feature here.
- “I want to compare three readers before choosing one.” → Only economically possible online.
- “It's 11pm and I can't stop turning this question over.” → Platforms run 24/7; local readers don't.

### Go in-person when…

- “My aunt's reader has been right for our family for years.” → A pre-validated reader beats any platform filter. Book the table.
- “I need this to feel like an occasion, not a transaction.” → The ritual is part of what you're buying. In-person delivers it.
- “I want someone to read me — not just my question.” → Presence carries information a chat window can't.

## Decision tree — pick your channel

1. **Do you already have a specific local reader you trust?** Yes → in-person, and this guide is moot. No → continue.
1. **Is this your first reading, or a first session with a new reader?** Yes → online. The refund window and the $20–$60 test are exactly built for this.
1. **Is privacy a factor in your question?** Yes → online chat or phone.
1. **Do you want a written record to reread?** Yes → online chat (transcript) over phone or table.
1. **Do you need the session to feel ceremonial to take it seriously?** Yes → in-person, once you've identified the reader through online validation or strong referral.
1. **Default if still torn:** online first. Validate the reader cheaply; upgrade the ritual later if it earns it.

## FAQ

**Are online psychics less accurate than in-person ones?
**

There's no evidence the channel itself changes accuracy. A reader who is generic across a table will be generic on video. What the channel changes is selection (you can find a better reader online), cost, and accountability. Choose the reader first; the channel second.

**Chat, phone, or video — which online format is best?
**

Chat gives you a written record and time to think, at the lowest rates — best for first sessions. Phone is the most conversational. Video adds face-to-face rapport at the highest per-minute rates. If in doubt: chat to test, phone once you know the reader fits.

**Can a psychic really read you without seeing you?
**

Practitioners say the connection isn't visual — and skeptics note that visual cues are exactly how cold reading works, so removing them is a stricter test, not a weaker one. Either way, a remote reading that produces verifiable specifics without seeing you is more impressive evidence, not less.

**How do I find a good local in-person reader?
**

Referral beats search. Ask people you trust who've actually paid for sessions, then apply the same checklist as online: specialization, transparent session pricing, no guarantees, no curse talk. If a local reader diagnoses a curse in session one and sells the cure, walk out — proximity is not legitimacy. See [the legitimacy checklist](https://mysticdo.com/guides/is-online-psychic-legit).

This comparison follows MysticDo's content methodology: Problem → Context → Options → Differences → Risks → Decision Criteria → Recommendation Path → Action. Prices reflect publicly listed rates at time of writing and are indicative. See [methodology](https://mysticdo.com/methodology).

# How Much Does a Psychic Reading Cost?

> Source: https://mysticdo.com/guides/psychic-reading-cost

Decision guide · Intent level 4 — Purchase
The advertised rate is rarely what you pay. Here's the full price structure — per-minute platforms, per-session independents, flat reports — and the one behavior that decides your real total.

Updated: September 2026 · Reading time: ~6 min

### Direct answer

A first psychic reading typically costs **$20–$60** on a per-minute platform (15–20 focused minutes, often with an intro offer) or **$60–$300** as a flat session with an independent reader. The rate matters less than the drift: an unfocused session at $3/min costs more than a sharp one at $8/min. Set a hard time budget before you connect.

### Key takeaways

- **Three pricing models exist**: per-minute platforms ($1–$15/min), per-session independents ($60–$300), and flat-fee reports or AI readings ($5–$50).
- **A sensible first session costs $20–$60** — 15–20 minutes with one specific question.
- **“Free minutes” are a sample, not a reading** — they're designed to convert you, so plan what you'll ask before they start.
- **Drift is the real cost driver** — vague questions and open-ended chat inflate any rate.
- **Price is a weak quality signal** — expensive readers are not reliably better; specialization and reviews matter more.

## The three pricing models

**Pricing snapshot — checked September 2026.** Ranges reflect publicly listed prices across major platforms and independent readers; per-provider sources will be linked as provider reviews publish. [How we track pricing](https://mysticdo.com/methodology#research).

Psychic readings are sold in three structures. Each has a different cost logic — and a different way of quietly overspending.

| Model | Typical price | What a first session costs | Where the overspend happens |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Per-minute platform (chat / phone / video) | $1–$15 per minute; intro offers often $1–$3/min | $20–$60 for 15–20 focused minutes | The clock runs while you think, type, or get comfortable — drift |
| Per-session independent reader | $60–$300 per session (30–60 min) | $60–$150 for a standard session; $200+ for well-known readers | Upsells: extended sessions, follow-up packages, “energy work” add-ons |
| Flat-fee report / AI reading | $5–$50 one-off | $5–$30 total | Buying report after report because each one is generic — you wanted a conversation, not a document |

The models aren't interchangeable. Per-minute buys you responsiveness — follow-up questions answered in real time. Per-session buys you structure — a beginning, middle, and end. A flat report buys you a document to reread. Paying per-minute for what a report does (or buying a report for what needs a conversation) is the most common way to feel you overpaid.

## What a session actually costs — worked examples

Rates mean little until you multiply them by minutes. Here's what platform sessions really total at common rates:

| Session length | At $2/min | At $5/min | At $10/min |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 10 minutes (one sharp question) | $20 | $50 | $100 |
| 20 minutes (question + follow-ups) | $40 | $100 | $200 |
| 40 minutes (drifted, open-ended) | $80 | $200 | $400 |

Read the third row carefully. Nothing about the service changed — only the focus did. A 10-minute session at $10/min and a 40-minute session at $2/min can deliver the same amount of useful content; one costs $100, the other $80 and four times your evening. This is why every guide on this site repeats the same rule: **the question does most of the work**, and the time budget does the rest.

## Intro offers and “free minutes” — how they really work

Most large platforms offer new customers something like “3 free minutes” or “$1/min for the first 10 minutes.” These are legitimate discounts, but they are designed as conversion funnels, not gifts. Three things to know:

- **The free minutes start the moment you connect.** If you spend them explaining your background, the paid clock starts before your actual question does. Write your question down before you connect and open with it.
- **Intro rates expire.** The same reader often costs 3–5× more on your second session. Judge the reader at the full rate, not the intro rate — that's what continuing with them actually costs.
- **Some offers require a deposit or card on file.** That's standard for the industry, but check the cancellation and refund terms before entering payment details. A platform with no visible refund policy is a platform to avoid at any price.

## The real cost driver: drift

Drift is what happens when a session has no sharp question and no time limit. It looks like this: you connect with a vague worry, the reader asks open questions, you tell the story, the reader reflects it back, twenty minutes pass, and you hang up with nothing you didn't already know. Drift is not always the reader's fault — but some readers rely on it, because a drifting client is a paying client.

The anti-drift protocol costs nothing:

1. **One specific question, written down** before you connect. “What's the actual dynamic between me and my ex right now?” not “tell me about my love life.”
1. **A hard time budget** — decide “15 minutes, then I end it” and say it out loud at the start.
1. **Minimal context up front.** Let the reader bring specifics; don't narrate the whole story on your own dime.
1. **End early if it's generic.** Reputable platforms refund or credit unsatisfactory first minutes. Using that policy is not rude — it's what it's for.

## Does a higher price mean a better reading?

Not reliably. Price in this market reflects positioning, demand, and platform tiering more than any verified skill hierarchy — there is no licensing body or certification that prices can point to. What a higher price *sometimes* correlates with: a reader with years of platform history, a full calendar (which limits drift — they're not incentivized to stretch your session), and a specialization. What it does not guarantee: accuracy, honesty, or fit for your question.

The evidence-backed quality signals are behavioral, not financial: a stated specialization that matches your question, a review distribution with credible mid-range reviews, transparent pricing, and a visible refund policy. A $3/min reader with those signals beats a $12/min reader without them. The full selection framework is in [How to Choose a Psychic Reader](https://mysticdo.com/guides/how-to-choose-psychic-reader).

## Real situations — what to budget

### Sensible budgets

- “I want a read on one specific situation before I decide something.” → Platform, one specific question, 15 minutes, intro rate: **$20–$45**. This is the highest-value purchase in the category.
- “I've found a reader I trust and want a deeper session on a big decision.” → Independent, structured 45–60 min session: **$100–$200**, booked after a cheaper first session proved the fit.
- “I'm curious what the format even feels like.” → [Free daily card](https://mysticdo.com/tools/daily-card) or a $5–$15 AI report. Don't pay human rates for curiosity.

### Budgets that usually end in regret

- Open-ended “let's see what comes up” sessions at per-minute rates — the classic $150+ drift.
- Weekly readings on the same unresolved question — at that point the cost belongs in a conversation with a counselor, not a reader.
- Any session where the reader introduces a new paid problem mid-reading (a “block,” a “curse,” an “attachment”) — that's not a price, it's a script. End the session.

## Decision tree — set your number before you connect

1. **Is your question still vague?** Yes → spend $0. Take the [Do What Fits](https://mysticdo.com/do-what-fits) matcher first.
1. **Do you want a conversation or a document?** Document → flat report ($5–$50). Conversation → continue.
1. **First time with this reader?** Yes → per-minute platform with a refund policy, 15-minute cap, intro rate if available. Budget $20–$60.
1. **Proven reader, bigger question?** Yes → per-session independent, fixed price agreed up front. Budget $100–$200.
1. **Did the session turn generic in the first 5 minutes?** Yes → end it and use the platform's refund or credit policy. The cheapest reading is the one you don't finish.

## FAQ

**Is $1 per minute too cheap to be good?
**

Not necessarily — intro offers often start at $1–$3/min from readers who normally charge more. Judge the reader at their standard rate, since that's what a second session costs. A permanently rock-bottom rate with no platform history, thin profile, and no reviews is a different matter: that's a signal, not a bargain.

**Why do some readers charge $15+ per minute?
**

Positioning and demand, mostly. High-rate readers usually have long platform tenure and full calendars. That can mean less incentive to stretch your session — but it does not certify skill. There is no licensing body in this industry, so price is a weak quality signal. Weigh specialization and review distribution first.

**Are “3 free minutes” actually free?
**

The minutes are real, but they start when you connect — so any time you spend on background burns them. They're a sample designed to convert you into a paying session. Write your question down first and open with it. Some offers also require a card on file, so read the refund terms before entering payment details.

**What's a reasonable monthly budget for readings?
**

For most people, occasional is the right cadence: one focused session when a real decision is on the table — call it $20–$60 a few times a year. If you're booking weekly on the same question, the reading has stopped being a decision tool and become an expense loop. That's the point to pause, not to upgrade.

**Do platforms or independents give better value?
**

Different value. Platforms give you per-minute flexibility, intro rates, and refund mechanisms — better for first sessions. Independents give you a structured, unhurried session at a fixed price — better once you know a reader fits you. The common path is platform first, independent later. See [online vs in-person](https://mysticdo.com/guides/online-psychic-vs-in-person) for the format trade-offs.

Prices reflect publicly listed platform rates at time of writing and are indicative; providers change pricing frequently, so verify on the provider's site before purchasing. Affiliate links, where present on linked pages, do not influence this guide's recommendations. See the [methodology page](https://mysticdo.com/methodology).

# Psychic vs Medium: The Difference That Actually Matters

> Source: https://mysticdo.com/guides/psychic-vs-medium

Comparison · Intent level 3
The two labels are often blurred in marketing — “psychic medium” sells better than either alone. But they do different jobs, and booking the wrong one for a grief question is the most expensive confusion in this category.

Updated: September 2026 · Reading time: ~5 min

### Direct answer

A **psychic** reads you and your situation — relationships, decisions, dynamics, likely directions. A **medium** claims to relay communication from people who have died. All mediums work psychically; most psychics do not practice mediumship. If your question is about the living, book a psychic. If it's about someone who passed, book a medium — and vet them harder, because grief is where this industry's worst actors hunt.

### Key takeaways

- **Psychic = reads the living.** Medium = claims contact with the dead. The overlap is technique, not purpose.
- **“Psychic medium” as a label tells you nothing** — ask which job you actually need done.
- **Mediumship questions are grief questions** — the emotional stakes change both the value and the risk.
- **Medium sessions cost more** ($75–$300+ vs $20–$60 for a first psychic session) and the vetting matters more.
- **The red flags are harsher in mediumship** — anyone who claims the deceased demands more paid sessions is exploiting grief. Full stop.

## The full comparison

| Dimension | Psychic reading | Medium reading |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Subject | You and the living people in your life — relationships, decisions, dynamics | People who have died — claimed communication with them |
| Best question type | “What's going on in this situation? What am I not seeing? What are my options?” | “Is there anything unresolved between us? Are they at peace? Do they have a message?” |
| Output form | Perspective on your situation — conversational, responsive | Claimed evidential details (names, memories, mannerisms) plus messages |
| Emotional register | Decision-support — clarity, options, next steps | Grief-adjacent — comfort, closure, continued bond |
| Typical price | $1–$15/min (platforms); $60–$300/session (independent) | $75–$300+/session; platform mediums $2–$15/min |
| Best for | Love, career, and life-direction questions about the living | Grief, unresolved loss, the sense of unfinished conversation |
| Limitations | Cannot contact the dead (and honest psychics say so); weak on timing | Unverifiable by nature; highest fraud density in the industry; not a substitute for grief support |

## Why the confusion exists — and who profits from it

Blur is commercially convenient. “Psychic medium” casts the widest net: it captures the relationship-anxiety searcher *and* the grief searcher with one profile. Platforms have no incentive to disambiguate, and many readers genuinely offer both — mediumship and psychic reading are related crafts, and some practitioners are honest about doing each in different sessions.

But the confusion costs you in a specific way: the two session types have **opposite vetting priorities**. A psychic session is judged on usefulness — did the perspective help your decision? A medium session is judged on evidence — did the reader produce specific details they couldn't have known? Booking a “psychic medium” without knowing which job you're buying means you can't evaluate what you got.

## Decision rule — which one does your question need?

| If your question is… | Pick |
| --- | --- |
| “Does my ex still think about me? Should I reach out?” | Psychic |
| “Is this job offer right? What's the dynamic on this team?” | Psychic |
| “My mother died and we never resolved things. Is she at peace?” | Medium |
| “I keep sensing my late father's presence. Am I imagining it?” | Medium — or, honestly, a grief counselor first if the question is consuming you |
| “I want to know what my future holds.” | Neither — that's a timing question; see [astrology](https://mysticdo.com/astrology/), with realistic expectations |
| “I'm not sure whether I need comfort or clarity.” | Take the [medium quiz](https://mysticdo.com/quiz/medium) — it separates the two before you spend |

## The grief premium — why mediumship needs harder vetting

Everything in the psychic red-flag list applies to mediums, plus a sharper set, because the client is grieving and the claims are unfalsifiable:

### Mediumship-specific red flags

- **The deceased “demands” more sessions.** Any claim that your loved one needs you to keep paying is grief exploitation — the single clearest walk-away signal in the category.
- **Only you can lift their unrest** — a curse script wearing grief's clothes. The deceased being “trapped” until you pay for ritual work is a documented scam pattern.
- **Fishing disguised as evidence.** “I'm getting a J name… John? James? A father figure?” — that's cold reading on the most vulnerable audience there is. Real evidential mediumship produces specifics you didn't feed.
- **Guaranteed contact.** Even the most credentialed working mediums describe connection as variable. “I will reach them, guaranteed” is a promise no honest practitioner makes.

And one honest note in the other direction: a medium session that produces comfort without verifiable specifics isn't automatically fraud — grief work is complicated, and many people value the ritual. The line is crossed when comfort becomes a meter running on your loss. For the full vetting protocol, see [the medium reading guide](https://mysticdo.com/guides/medium-reading-guide).

## Can one session do both?

Sometimes — and this is the legitimate version of “psychic medium.” A common honest format: the session opens with evidential mediumship (attempted contact, specific details), then shifts to psychic guidance about your life now. If a reader offers this, the healthy framing is two products in one appointment — evaluate each half by its own standard. Evidence for the first; usefulness for the second.

If you're early in grief — raw, recent loss — consider waiting. Not because mediumship is wrong, but because the rawest stage is when you're least able to evaluate what you're buying. The reading will still be available in three months. The [Loss & Closure page](https://mysticdo.com/questions/loss-closure/) walks through the timing question in more detail.

## FAQ

**Are mediums more “gifted” than psychics?
**

Practitioners frame mediumship as a specialization, not a promotion — like a surgeon versus a GP. Some psychics train for years and never work with the deceased; some mediums do no general psychic work at all. Judge each by their own job: evidence for mediums, usefulness for psychics. “More gifted” is marketing language.

**How do I know if a medium actually reached my loved one?
**

You can't verify it — that's the honest answer. What you can evaluate is evidence quality: specific, unusual, correct details you didn't provide (a nickname, an object, a private joke) versus high-probability generalities (“he watches over you,” “she's proud of you”). The first is interesting; the second is available at any price, including free. Keep your bar where you set it before the session, not where emotion moves it during.

**Is online mediumship as good as in-person?
**

Practitioners say the connection isn't physical, and there's a structural argument that remote is a stricter test — the reader can't watch your face for reactions. The bigger variable is accountability: platform sessions have refund windows and review histories; a famous in-person medium has neither. Whatever the channel, the evidential bar stays the same.

**Should I see a medium or a grief counselor?
**

They answer different needs, and one is regulated while the other isn't. If grief is disrupting your sleep, work, or ability to function — counselor first, no hesitation. A medium reading addresses the spiritual question (continued bond, unresolved words), not the psychological one (processing loss). Many people use both; the order matters. Mediumship is not therapy and no ethical medium claims otherwise.

This comparison follows MysticDo's content methodology: Problem → Context → Options → Differences → Risks → Decision Criteria → Recommendation Path → Action. MysticDo does not verify survival-of-consciousness claims; this guide evaluates service honesty and usefulness only. Prices reflect publicly listed rates at time of writing and are indicative. See [methodology](https://mysticdo.com/methodology).

# Psychic vs Tarot: Which Fits Your Question?

> Source: https://mysticdo.com/guides/psychic-vs-tarot

Comparison · Intent level 3
They answer different questions. A psychic gives you an outside read on a specific person or situation. Tarot gives you a structured mirror for reflecting on a dynamic or pattern. Picking the wrong one wastes your money.

Updated: September 2026 · Reading time: ~5 min

### Direct answer

Choose **psychic** when you have a specific question about a person or situation and want a direct, responsive read. Choose **tarot** when you want a structured reflection on dynamics, decisions, or patterns. If you want timing or long-arc patterns, neither is ideal — see [astrology](https://mysticdo.com/astrology/).

### Key takeaways

- **Psychic answers**: “What's going on with this person / situation right now?”
- **Tarot answers**: “What's the pattern / dynamic / angle I'm not seeing?”
- **Psychic is conversational**; tarot is structured-symbolic.
- **They overlap** on relationship questions — but the right choice depends on whether you want a read on someone else (psychic) or a map of the dynamic (tarot).
- **Many readers do both**, but rarely equally well. Match the tool to the question, not the reader to the title.

## The full comparison

Here's how they differ across the dimensions that actually matter for your decision.

| Dimension | Psychic reading | Tarot reading |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Best question type | Direct question about a person or situation — “what's going on with X?” | Reflective question about dynamics or patterns — “what's the pattern here?” |
| Output form | Conversational, responsive, intuitive | Symbolic interpretation of laid cards in a spread |
| Personalization | Highly personalized, in the moment | Personalized through the spread's positions, not the reader's intuition |
| Time scale | Current situation — what's happening now | Situational — past/present/obstacle/option within a question |
| Typical price | $1–$15/min (platforms); $60–$300/session (independent) | $1–$8/min (platforms); $30–$150/session (independent) |
| Best for | People with a specific question who want an outside angle they can't generate alone | People who want to reflect on a dynamic or decision through a structured framework |
| Limitations | Vague if your question is vague; not built for timing or pattern reflection; fraud risk higher | Symbolic and interpretive — two readers may read the same cards differently; not built for direct reads on another person |
| Free first step | Intent quiz to confirm fit; this decision guide | Daily card pull to feel the format; intent quiz to confirm fit |

## Decision rule — which one fits your question?

Use this rule of thumb. If your question is closer to column A, psychic fits. If closer to column B, tarot fits.

| If your question is… | Pick |
| --- | --- |
| “What does [person] actually feel / want right now?” | Psychic |
| “Will [person] reach out?” | Psychic (with realistic expectations) |
| “What's the dynamic between us that I'm not seeing?” | Tarot |
| “I keep repeating this pattern in relationships — why?” | Tarot |
| “Should I take this job offer?” | Either — psychic for an outside read, tarot for a structured reflection on the two paths |
| “When will I meet someone?” | Neither — try [astrology](https://mysticdo.com/astrology/), or accept that no tool reliably answers timing |

## When one beats the other

### Psychic wins when…

- You have a specific person or situation you want a direct read on.
- You want conversational follow-up — to redirect, probe, clarify in the moment.
- You want a perspective, not a symbolic map.

### Tarot wins when…

- You want to reflect on a dynamic or decision rather than be told.
- You're working with recurring patterns, not a single moment.
- You want a structured framework (past / present / obstacle / option) to think through.
- You prefer a written record (a spread can be photographed and revisited).

## What if both fit?

Some questions sit between them. A career decision can be a psychic read (“what's really going on with this team?”) or a tarot spread (“two paths — what does each actually involve?”). If both fit and you can only do one, ask yourself: do I want a direct answer, or a structured reflection? Direct → psychic. Reflection → tarot.

If you genuinely can't decide, start with the cheaper, lower-stakes option: the [free daily card](https://mysticdo.com/tools/daily-card) to feel the tarot format, or a 10-minute psychic session to feel the conversational format. Then re-decide.

## FAQ

**Is a psychic more accurate than tarot?
**

Neither is “accurate” in a forecasting sense. They produce different kinds of output. Psychic produces a perspective on a specific question; tarot produces a structured reflection. Compare them on fit, not accuracy.

**Can one reader do both?
**

Some readers offer both. Most do one better than the other. If you want tarot, find a tarot specialist; if you want psychic, find a psychic specialist. All-in-one readers often do neither well.

**Which is cheaper?
**

Tarot tends to be cheaper per session. Independent tarot readers run $30–$150; psychic readers $60–$300. Both have per-minute platform options.

**Should I do tarot first if I'm not sure what I'm asking?
**

Yes — tarot's structured spread can help you discover the actual question. Or take the [intent quiz](https://mysticdo.com/do-what-fits) first, which costs nothing.

# How Much Does a Tarot Reading Cost?

> Source: https://mysticdo.com/guides/tarot-reading-cost

Decision guide · Intent level 4 — Purchase
Tarot is the cheapest entry point in spiritual services — and still easy to overpay for. Here's the real price structure, what each tier buys, and when free is genuinely enough.

Updated: September 2026 · Reading time: ~6 min

### Direct answer

A tarot reading costs **$1–$8 per minute** on platforms (a focused first session: $15–$45), **$30–$150 per session** with an independent reader, and **$0–$30** for apps and AI readings. Tarot runs cheaper than psychic readings at every tier. The sweet spot for a first paid reading is a 15–20 minute platform session with a tarot specialist — not the biggest spread on the menu.

### Key takeaways

- **Tarot is priced below psychic at every tier** — the skill is structured and teachable, so supply is wider.
- **A sensible first paid reading costs $15–$45** — 15–20 minutes, one question, one spread.
- **Bigger spread ≠ better reading.** A focused 3-card spread on a sharp question beats a $200 Celtic Cross on a vague one.
- **Free tools cover the exploration stage** — daily pulls and apps are legitimately useful until you need interactive interpretation.
- **Pay for interpretation, not card-turning.** An app can turn cards. What you're paying a human for is the synthesis across positions, applied to your situation.

## The price structure

**Pricing snapshot — checked September 2026.** Ranges reflect publicly listed prices across major platforms and independent readers; per-provider sources will be linked as provider reviews publish. [How we track pricing](https://mysticdo.com/methodology#research).

Tarot is sold in four formats, each with its own logic:

| Format | Typical price | What it buys | Best for |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Platform per-minute (chat / phone / video) | $1–$8/min; intro offers from ~$1/min | Live interactive reading; follow-up questions in real time | First readings, specific questions, testing readers |
| Independent per-session | $30–$150 (30–60 min); known readers $150+ | Structured session, often with a written summary or photo of the spread | Deeper sessions with a reader you've validated |
| Recorded / email reading | $15–$60 flat | A video or written reading you can reread; no live interaction | People who want a document, not a conversation |
| Apps & AI readings | Free – $30 | Instant card pulls with templated interpretations | Exploration, learning the cards, low-stakes reflection |

For comparison, psychic readings run $1–$15/min and $60–$300/session. Tarot's lower ceiling reflects supply: competent tarot readers are far more common than readers who can sustain a purely intuitive session. That works in your favor — at the $30–$80 tier, tarot arguably delivers the most structured insight per dollar in the category.

## What the money actually buys at each tier

The mistake is thinking you're paying for cards. Cards are free — a deck costs $20 and apps cost nothing. You're paying for three things, and each tier delivers them differently:

1. **Spread structure.** Matching the spread to the question (3-card for a decision, relationship spread for a dynamic, Celtic Cross for a full situation map). Free tools do this mechanically; good readers do it diagnostically.
1. **Synthesis.** Reading the cards against each other — how the obstacle card modifies the outcome card — instead of reciting one meaning per position. This is the core skill, and it's what separates a $3/min reader from a $0 app.
1. **Application.** Connecting the synthesis to your actual situation and your actual decision. Only a live human in conversation can do this fully. This is the thing worth paying for — and the thing to test in a first session.

If a reading delivers layer 1 only, you overpaid at any price — an app does that. Layer 2 is worth $15–$45. Layer 3 is what makes a $100 session worth it.

## Free vs. paid — where the line actually is

Tarot has the best free tier in spiritual services, and it would be dishonest to pretend otherwise:

- **Daily single-card pulls** (including [ours](https://mysticdo.com/tools/daily-card)) teach you how symbolic reflection feels. Free, and genuinely useful.
- **App spreads with templated meanings** cover self-reflection on low-stakes questions. Free to $10.
- **Learning to read your own cards** is a legitimate path — a deck and a guidebook cost less than one mid-tier session.

The line where paying makes sense: when your question is specific, emotionally loaded, or high-stakes enough that you want *interactive* interpretation — someone who can answer “but what does the Seven of Swords in the obstacle position mean for *my* no-contact situation, specifically?” Apps don't do that. A $20 platform session does.

## Real situations — what to budget

### Sensible budgets

- “I keep having the same relationship pattern and want to see it mapped.” → Platform, tarot specialist, 20 minutes, relationship spread: **$20–$45**.
- “Big decision — two job paths — and I want a full picture with a reader I already trust.” → Independent, 45–60 min, Celtic Cross or two-path spread: **$80–$150**.
- “I'm just curious how tarot works.” → [Free daily card](https://mysticdo.com/tools/daily-card) for a week, then an app. Total: **$0–$10**.

### Budgets that usually end in regret

- The biggest spread on the menu for a first session — you're paying Celtic Cross prices before you know if the reader can synthesize.
- Pulling paid readings on the same question repeatedly until the cards “agree” — that's not a budget, it's a loop.
- Per-minute drift on a platform: “let's pull a few more cards on that” at $6/min adds up faster than any flat session.

## Decision tree — set your tarot budget

1. **Still exploring what tarot even does?** Yes → $0. Daily card + an app for a week.
1. **Is your question specific and you want live interpretation?** Yes → platform, tarot specialist, 15–20 min cap. Budget $15–$45.
1. **Do you want a document rather than a conversation?** Yes → recorded/email reading, $15–$60 flat.
1. **Have you validated a reader and want depth?** Yes → independent session, fixed price agreed up front, $80–$150.
1. **Did the reader recite one meaning per card with no synthesis?** Yes → that's layer-1 reading. End early, use the refund window, and don't rebook at any price.

## FAQ

**Is a $5 tarot reading worth it?
**

At $5 you're getting either a new reader building reviews or a templated app-style reading with a human wrapper. It can be a fine format test, but don't judge tarot as a practice by the $5 tier — the synthesis that makes readings valuable rarely survives at that price.

**Why do some tarot readers charge $200+?
**

Reputation, demand, and positioning — same as any consultative service. Some well-known readers with years of public track record justify it. But price is not a quality certification: a $40 platform specialist with strong reviews in your question type often out-delivers a famous generalist. Match the reader to the question, not the price to your anxiety.

**Are free tarot apps as good as paid readings?
**

For card meanings and self-reflection, yes — the deck doesn't care who shuffles. What apps can't do is interactive synthesis: weighing positions against each other and applying them to your specific situation in real time. That's the entire value of a paid human reading. If you don't need that layer, don't pay for it.

**How many cards should a first reading use?
**

Three to ten. A 3-card spread handles one decision; a relationship spread (5–7 cards) maps a dynamic; a Celtic Cross (10) maps a full situation. Anything larger on a first session is usually padding. The reader should explain why the spread fits your question — if they can't, the spread is theater.

**Should I tip a tarot reader?
**

On platforms, no — the rate is the rate, and the platform takes its cut either way. With independents, tipping isn't expected but is a reasonable gesture for an exceptional session. What readers value more: a specific, honest review.

# Tarot vs Astrology: Which Fits Your Question?

> Source: https://mysticdo.com/guides/tarot-vs-astrology

Comparison · Intent level 3
They look interchangeable from the outside and aren't. Tarot is a mirror for the present situation. Astrology is a map of long-arc patterns and timing. Booking the wrong one is the most common way to leave a reading disappointed.

Updated: September 2026 · Reading time: ~5 min

### Direct answer

Choose **tarot** for questions about a current situation — a decision, a dynamic, a pattern you want reflected now. Choose **astrology** for questions about timing, life-arc patterns, compatibility, and the longer cycle you're inside. If your question starts with “when,” astrology is the only one of the two even attempting an answer.

### Key takeaways

- **Tarot answers**: “What's going on in this situation right now, and what angle am I missing?”
- **Astrology answers**: “What cycle am I in, when does it shift, and how am I wired for this?”
- **Tarot is generated fresh per question**; astrology is computed from your birth data — same chart, many readings.
- **Tarot is cheaper per session** ($15–$45 typical); a real natal reading runs $100–$300 but stays relevant for years.
- **They combine well in sequence** — astrology for the map, tarot for the moment inside the map.

## The full comparison

| Dimension | Tarot reading | Astrology reading |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Best question type | Current situations — a decision, a dynamic, “what am I not seeing?” | Timing, life-arc patterns, compatibility, “when” and “why am I wired this way?” |
| Input | Your question + a shuffled deck — generated fresh each time | Your birth date, time, and place — one fixed chart, interpreted many ways |
| Output form | Symbolic reflection on the present: a spread with interacting positions | Structured analysis: natal placements, transits, cycles — often a report or recorded session |
| Time scale | Now to near-term — this situation, this month | Months to decades — life chapters, year-ahead transits, Saturn returns |
| Typical price | $1–$8/min (platforms); $30–$150/session (independent) | $50–$150 (report-style); $100–$300 (live natal reading); horoscopes free |
| Best for | People who want an interactive reflection on something happening now | People who want a durable framework for their patterns and timing |
| Limitations | Weak on timing; same question re-pulled gives different cards; quality depends entirely on reader synthesis | Requires accurate birth time for full precision; not built for “what should I do today”; readings can feel impersonal if the astrologer stays technical |
| Free first step | [Daily card pull](https://mysticdo.com/tools/daily-card) | Free natal chart generators — see the map before paying for the tour |

## Decision rule — match the question to the tool

| If your question is… | Pick |
| --- | --- |
| “Should I take this job / end this relationship / make this move?” | Tarot — it's a present-tense decision |
| “When will things turn around for me?” | Astrology — timing is its core product |
| “Why do I keep repeating this pattern across relationships / jobs?” | Either — tarot for the current loop, astrology for the lifelong wiring |
| “Are we compatible?” | Astrology (synastry) — tarot can read the current dynamic, not the structural fit |
| “What's the dynamic between me and this person right now?” | Tarot — or a psychic, if you want a direct read rather than a reflection |
| “What should I focus on this year?” | Astrology — a transit / year-ahead reading is exactly this |

## When one beats the other

### Tarot wins when…

- The question is about *now* — a live decision, a current dynamic, this week's crossroads.
- You want interaction — to pull a clarifier, redirect, ask “but what about the other option?”
- You don't know your exact birth time (astrology's precision collapses without it; tarot doesn't care).
- Budget is tight — a useful tarot session starts around $20.

### Astrology wins when…

- The question has a *when* in it — timing is the one thing tarot structurally can't do.
- You want something durable — a natal chart is computed once and reinterpreted for decades; a tarot spread dissolves when the session ends.
- You want depth on who you are, not just what to do — strengths, blind spots, relational wiring.
- You prefer a document — many astrologers deliver written or recorded readings you can revisit for years.

## What if both fit?

Sequence them — in this order. Start with astrology for the map: what cycle you're in, what this year is structurally about, how you're wired for the decision. Then use tarot for the moment inside the map: this offer, this person, this week. Astrology tells you it's a year for consolidation; tarot tells you whether *this specific* consolidation move is clean.

The reverse order wastes money: pulling tarot cards on a timing question produces vague cards, and buying a $200 natal reading to answer “should I text him back?” is a map bought for a footstep.

And if your question is really “what is this other person thinking or feeling right now?” — neither tool is built for that. That's the psychic use case; see [Psychic vs Tarot](https://mysticdo.com/guides/psychic-vs-tarot).

## FAQ

**Which is more accurate, tarot or astrology?
**

They aren't competing forecasts — they're different instruments. Tarot reflects a present situation; astrology maps long-arc patterns. Judge each on whether its output was useful for its own job: did the spread illuminate the decision? Did the chart reading describe your patterns with uncomfortable precision? “Accuracy” across the two categories isn't a meaningful comparison.

**Can one practitioner do both?
**

Some do, and a few do both well — but they are different crafts. Tarot rewards improvisational synthesis; astrology rewards years of technical study. If you're buying a natal reading, buy it from someone whose practice is astrology-first. If you're buying a spread, buy it from a tarot-first reader. The all-in-one practitioner often peaks in one and pads the other.

**I don't know my birth time. Is astrology off the table?
**

Partially. Sun, Moon (roughly), and most planetary placements can still be read — but the Ascendant and house system, which govern timing and life areas, need an accurate time. Some astrologers offer chart rectification (estimating birth time from life events) as a paid service. If that's not worth it to you, tarot needs nothing but a question.

**Are daily horoscopes a cheap substitute for an astrology reading?
**

No — horoscopes are written for one-twelfth of humanity. They're entertainment with occasional resonance. A real astrology reading is computed from your exact birth data, which is why it costs $100+ and a horoscope costs nothing. See [Astrology Reading vs Horoscope](https://mysticdo.com/guides/astrology-reading-vs-horoscope) for the full breakdown.

# Medium Readings

> Source: https://mysticdo.com/medium/

Category · Level 1–5 coverage
A medium reading is for **navigating loss and seeking connection or closure** — not for general life questions. The category deserves particular care: grief is real, vulnerability is high, and the difference between a responsible medium and a manipulative one is wide.

[Take the medium quiz →](https://mysticdo.com/quiz/medium) [Not sure? Do What Fits](https://mysticdo.com/do-what-fits)
[What it does](#what) [Psychic vs medium](#vs-psychic) [Who it's for](#who) [Questions to ask](#questions) [How to choose](#choose) [Providers](#providers)
What it does
## A medium reading, in one paragraph

A medium attempts to connect with someone who has died and convey messages or a sense of presence to the living person. Whether you treat this as literal or symbolic, the value people report is often less about “facts” and more about a felt sense of connection, meaning, or things-left-unsaid finally reaching expression.

### The short version

A medium reading fits when you are **navigating loss** and want connection or closure. It does not fit for general life questions (try psychic), reflective pattern-spotting (try tarot), or timing (try astrology).

The key distinction
## Psychic vs medium — the difference that matters

These are not the same service. A psychic reads your situation; a medium attempts to reach someone who has passed. Not all psychics are mediums, and not all mediums read current life situations well.

| Dimension | Psychic | Medium |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Reads | Your current situation, people, decisions | Connection to someone who has passed |
| Best question | “What's going on with X right now?” | “Is there anything from [person] I haven't heard?” |
| Risk if misused | Wasted money on vague reads | Exploitation of grief; false hope |
| Vetting needed | Moderate — specialization, pricing | High — fraud risk is real, emotional stakes are high |
| Overlap | Some psychics are also mediums | Some mediums also do psychic work |

For the full comparison — including which questions fit which service and the grief-specific vetting rules — see [Psychic vs Medium](https://mysticdo.com/guides/psychic-vs-medium).

Who it's for
## It fits when…

- **You are navigating grief** and want a sense of connection, not necessarily facts.
- **There are things left unsaid** and you want a space for that, regardless of literal truth.
- **You're past the acute stage** and considering meaning-making, not crisis support.

### It does *not* fit when…

- You are in acute crisis — a medium is not a substitute for grief counseling or therapy.
- You want a guarantee of contact. No responsible medium guarantees a specific connection.
- You're seeking general life guidance — that's psychic, tarot, or astrology.

Questions to ask
## What to bring to a medium reading

### Approach the session with

- An open name or initial of the person — not a flood of biographical detail. Let the medium bring specifics, not you.
- One or two things left unsaid you'd want to express or hear acknowledged.
- Permission to yourself that the session may not produce the contact you hoped for — and that's not a verdict on the person you lost.
- A support person or follow-up plan, because readings can surface grief you didn't expect.

How to choose
## How to choose a medium — with extra care

Because the emotional stakes are high, the vetting bar is higher than for other categories.

1. **Look for evidence-based specifics** — a responsible medium offers verifiable details you didn't supply, not generic “I sense a father figure.”
1. **Watch for cold reading** — fishing questions (“does the letter M mean anything?”) that put words in your mouth.
1. **Refuse “curse” or “blockage” upsells** — the most common fraud pattern in this category.
1. **Read the refund policy before booking** — reputable mediums acknowledge sessions vary.

### Red flags

- Guaranteed contact with a specific person.
- “Energy clearing” or “curse removal” upsells attached to the session.
- Pressure to book longer or repeat sessions for “the connection to hold.”
- Refusal to let you bring a support person.

For the complete picture — session structure, costs, the evidence standard, and how to prepare — see [What Does a Medium Reading Actually Do?](https://mysticdo.com/guides/medium-reading-guide)

Provider research
## The providers we're evaluating

No recommendations yet — by design
No provider earns a place on this page until its review is complete — that's the bar our [methodology](https://mysticdo.com/methodology) sets. Because fraud risk runs higher in this category, the review standard adds extra vetting checks before any medium is listed.

Before you go

# Methodology & Trust

> Source: https://mysticdo.com/methodology

How we work
Spiritual services carry a real trust problem. We don't ask you to trust us. We show our work — where facts come from, how the quiz thinks, what AI does and doesn't do, how money flows, and where this site is still unfinished.

### At a glance

- **What we publish:** decision guides, comparisons, an intent quiz, and free tools — not horoscopes, not an encyclopedia, not a link farm.
- **Provider facts** come from the provider's own public pages, checked by us — never from reader-submitted bios or press releases.
- **Every claim has a class:** verified by us, platform-stated, user-reported, or editorial judgment. The difference is labeled, not blurred.
- **Affiliate links pay for the site.** They never decide rankings, and we say when free is enough — even when a paid option would earn us a commission.
- **AI is part of how this site is made.** What it doesn't do: decide conclusions, verify facts, or publish. A human does all three.
- **Honest current state.** Provider reviews are being written to the standard below and publish on a rolling basis; the quiz is rule-based. We'd rather say that plainly than let you discover it.

## The five questions

Before the details, the short answers to the five questions a methodology page exists to answer.

Who A small, independent project — not a company, an agency, or a content farm. Research and production are AI-assisted; a human reviews and approves everything before it publishes.

What The decision layer of spiritual services: which kind of guidance fits which situation, what things cost, how providers differ, and what to do next.

How Documented research: platform facts verified at the source, community signals read as patterns, structured editorial frameworks, and judgment that's labeled as judgment.

What we measure Fit (situation to service), price mechanics, transparency, safety patterns, and whether a service helps you ask a better question — not whether it's "true."

What we don't claim We don't claim any practice is real or fake, and nobody — including us — can guarantee a reading will help you. We help you decide what to do, not what to believe.

## Our position on spiritual services

MysticDo does not attempt to prove that any spiritual practice is "real" or "true." That question is outside our scope — and outside what someone deciding whether to spend $40 on a reading actually needs answered by us.

What we do take a position on:

- **If you decide to try a service**, we help you understand what it's for, who it suits, what it costs, and how to choose a provider.
- **We help you reduce unnecessary risk** — financial, emotional, and the risk of being manipulated by an industry that sometimes preys on people at their lowest.
- **We say when free is enough**, even when a paid option would earn us a commission.

## Who is behind MysticDo

MysticDo is a small, independent project. We are not a company, a media group, or a marketing agency, and we don't write as if we were. Research and production are AI-assisted — and a human reviews every page before it publishes.

This is also not our first site in this space. MysticDo grew out of an earlier, smaller psychic review project where the core of this model — decision-first content, documented methods, disclosed affiliate links — was tested against real visitors and real (small) revenue. That project is where we learned how expensive honest research is, and how much of this industry's "information" is marketing in a costume.

Two things carried over from that project: the method, and the lessons. One thing deliberately did not: **conclusions**. MysticDo's provider coverage starts from zero. When we reference industry patterns, we label the evidence level (see below). We don't inherit old verdicts — that would be exactly the kind of stale, unearned authority this page exists to prevent.

### How the work is divided

The pipeline is intentionally small and split into stages that cannot self-certify:

1. **Research stage** — gathering provider pricing pages, policy documents, and community-signal threads; assembling comparison data; drafting decision frameworks. AI-assisted for scale and consistency.
1. **Editorial review stage** — a human checks every material fact against its source, applies the evidence-level labels below, and decides what stays, what's downgraded, and what's cut. This stage cannot be skipped or automated.
1. **Publish stage** — only after editorial review signs off does a page go live. Pricing snapshots are dated at this step; corrections are logged in the changelog below.

The roles here are functional, not titular. We don't list individuals, because the trust model rests on the process — verifiable sources, labeled evidence, dated updates — not on a personality. When a real, externally verifiable identity is ready to stand behind specific pages, we'll say so plainly. Until then, the method is the byline.

## How we understand your intent

MysticDo is organized around what you're trying to decide, not around topics. We manage all content against a five-level intent model:

| Level | What the user is really asking | Example | Our investment |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 — Curiosity | "What is this?" | what is tarot | Brief context only; we don't chase this traffic |
| 2 — Problem | "Can this help me?" | can tarot help with a breakup | Explain fit honestly, including when the answer is no |
| 3 — Comparison | "Which of these?" | tarot vs psychic | Full comparison tables with mandatory limitations |
| 4 — Purchase validation | "Is this worth paying for? Is it legit?" | are online psychics legit, psychic reading cost | Decision guides — our core work |
| 5 — Action | "Who do I book?" | best site for a medium reading | Provider recommendations under the standard below |

Our resources concentrate on Levels 3–5. That is a deliberate editorial choice: the curiosity layer is drowning in generic content, while the decision layer — where you're about to spend money and want someone honest in the room — is barely served.

### How the intent quiz works — and what it isn't

[Do What Fits](https://mysticdo.com/do-what-fits) and the four category quizzes ask about your situation, not your birth data. Under the hood, the current version is a transparent rule-based matcher: your answers map to a small set of intent profiles (love, life direction, spiritual growth, loss), and each profile maps to the guidance formats that structurally fit that kind of question.

The quiz uses psychological relevance — questions that recognize your situation — to make guidance feel personal. This is a deliberate design choice, and it has a hard boundary: **relevance is not diagnosis.** When a result says "people in your situation often benefit from a reflective format," that's a pattern statement about many people, not a claim about you specifically. If you're in acute grief or crisis, the quiz points you to professional support before it points you to any service — because that's the one situation where a wrong recommendation costs more than money.

Its honest limits: it's rule-based, the question set is small, and it doesn't learn yet. Quiz results are a starting point for reading the right guide — never a verdict.

## Three kinds of content, three methods

MysticDo publishes structurally different content types. Each has its own method, because each answers a different question. We never apply one method to another's job.

Decision guides
### Editorial framework

Built on the eight-step structure below. A guide earns its place by walking your actual decision — not by covering a keyword.

Comparisons
### Dimension tables

Fixed dimensions, a mandatory limitations row, never a single "winner." The decision stays yours — see the comparison rules below.

Provider reviews
### Provider standard

A fixed 13-part template with a mandatory limitations section and dated price snapshots. None published yet — placeholders until they're real.

A fourth type, **free tools**, exists for reflection and practice — the [Daily Card Pull](https://mysticdo.com/tools/daily-card) is a prompt for thinking, not a reading, and the page says so. Tools never upsell; they point to guides when a card isn't enough.

## How a decision guide is built

Every commercial guide follows the same spine, because the reader's decision follows the same spine:

1. **Problem** — name the actual situation you're in, in your language, not industry jargon.
1. **Context** — what this kind of problem usually is, and what it usually isn't.
1. **Options** — the realistic paths: psychic, tarot, astrology, medium, free tools, or nothing.
1. **Differences** — what each path actually delivers: output format, personalization, time scale.
1. **Risks** — the financial and emotional failure modes, including how this niche gets exploited.
1. **Decision criteria** — the factors that should drive your choice, stated before any recommendation.
1. **Recommendation path** — situations mapped to paths. Plural paths, because one size fits nobody.
1. **Action** — the concrete next step, even when the next step is "don't spend money yet."

A guide that can't survive this structure usually isn't a decision guide — it's a sermon or a sales page. If you find one of ours that reads like either, that's a bug and we want to hear about it.

## How comparisons stay honest

Comparison pages are where most sites quietly sell. Ours follow fixed rules:

- **Never a "best" verdict.** Fit depends on your situation — that's the entire premise of this site.
- **Fixed dimensions:** what question it fits, output format, personalization, time scale, typical price, who it suits, and limitations.
- **The limitations row is mandatory.** A comparison without limitations is an advertisement with a table in it.
- **The decision stays with you.** Our job is to make the differences visible, not to choose for you. See [Psychic vs Tarot](https://mysticdo.com/guides/psychic-vs-tarot) for the pattern in practice.

## How we research

Every material fact on this site traces to a source, and every source has an update policy:

| Information type | Source | Update policy |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Provider pricing | The provider's own public pricing pages | Verified at time of writing; flagged if more than 6 months old |
| Provider features | The provider's own public documentation | Reviewed each update cycle |
| Reader specializations | The reader's stated specialties on the platform | As listed; never editorially assigned by us |
| Review distribution | Platform review aggregates | Snapshot at time of writing |
| Community signals | Forums, Reddit, review sites | Read as patterns, never as proof; revisited when the pattern shifts |
| User scenarios | Composite and illustrative — never real users | Labeled as fictional on every page that uses them |
| Comparative analysis | MysticDo editorial, clearly labeled | Updated when the underlying material facts change |

One rule disciplines all of it: **we check the source rather than cite the middleman.** When a price, policy, or feature matters to a decision, it gets verified on the provider's own platform before it enters a page. When we can't verify something, we say so — and the claim gets downgraded to the evidence level it deserves.

## Evidence levels: what we know vs. what we think

Not all statements on this site carry the same weight. Every material claim belongs to one of four classes, and the wording on the page is built to show you which is which:

Level 1 — Verified by us We checked it on the provider's platform ourselves: listed prices, policy pages, available formats, reader directory behavior.

Sounds like: "Chat rates start at $X per minute, as listed on reader profiles."

Level 2 — Platform-stated The provider says so; we haven't stress-tested it. Useful, but it's their voice, not ours.

Sounds like: "The platform states it screens every applicant."

Level 3 — User-reported Aggregated from reviews, forums, and community threads. Genuine signals; individually unverifiable.

Sounds like: "Refund complaints recur across independent review threads."

Level 4 — Editorial judgment Our interpretation, framed as interpretation. It can be well-reasoned; it cannot be a fact.

Sounds like: "For your situation, a reflective format may fit better than a predictive one."

The rule that makes this useful: **numbers come from Levels 1–2, and anything worded as "may fit" is Level 4.** If you ever see a hard number presented as our judgment, or a judgment dressed up as a number, the page has failed its own standard.

## Provider reviews: the standard we hold

Provider reviews are where trust matters most in this niche — so they're also where we're slowest. Every provider review published on MysticDo must complete a fixed template:

1. **Overview** — what the service offers, factually and neutrally.
1. **Who it may suit** — matched to question types, never "everyone."
1. **How the experience works** — format, flow, and what actually happens.
1. **Pricing structure** — with the date the prices were checked.
1. **Types of readers** — what specializations actually exist.
1. **Strengths** — what the service genuinely does well.
1. **Limitations** — where it falls short. This section is mandatory; a review without it is an ad.
1. **Best use cases** — which situations it fits.
1. **What to know before buying** — the gotchas and the checks.
1. **How this review was researched** — the evidence levels used, stated on the page.
1. **Alternative providers** — because a review with no alternatives is a sales funnel.
1. **FAQ** — the questions people actually ask.
1. **Next step** — where to go from here, including "not this one."

Why a fixed template? To prevent the affiliate-review death spiral: *five stars → five stars → "click here."* A template forces the sections marketing would rather skip — limitations, alternatives, and the difference between what a platform claims and what users report.

### Current status, stated plainly

- **Zero provider reviews are published today.** Provider sections across MysticDo are placeholders, and they say so on the page.
- When the first real reviews go live, each will state when prices were checked, what we verified versus what the platform claims, and which community signals we weighed.
- We would rather have an empty shelf than a fake one. This is a choice, and it costs us money every week it lasts.

### Why you won't find overall scores here

You will not see a "9.4/10" next to any provider on MysticDo. This is deliberate, and it's the one place we diverge from most comparison sites by design:

- **A single score implies precision that doesn't exist** for subjective services. "Accuracy" isn't measurable across readers, sessions, or the person asking.
- **Scores hide the dimension that matters to you.** If you care most about price, a composite rating built mostly on other things will mislead you confidently.
- **Numbers invite verdict-shopping.** We'd rather you comparison-think your situation than comparison-shop our conclusions.

Instead, provider pages carry **structured dimensions** — pricing mechanics, transparency, reader vetting, formats, red-flag patterns — and you do the weighting. This costs us the simplicity of a league table. We think it buys you something better.

## Language rules: what we will and won't say

Trust is built or lost sentence by sentence. We keep two house lists, and every page is checked against them.

### We write

- "This type of reading is commonly used for…"
- "People often choose this when…"
- "If your main question is X, this format may fit better than Y."
- "This may help you explore…"

### We don't write

- "This will tell you your future."
- "Guaranteed accurate" — about any service, including our own guidance.
- "The #1 psychic site of 2026."
- Testimonial framing we can't verify — "she knew everything about me."

Two standing rules sit underneath both lists. First, **we never promise outcomes** — from any service, or from us. Second, **we never write as if a practice's truth were settled**, in either direction: devout belief and reflexive mockery are both positions you're entitled to hold, and neither is a job description for a decision guide.

## How we use AI — exactly where, and where it stops

MysticDo is upfront about this: AI is part of how this site gets made. We use it for research assistance — clustering community threads, surfacing recurring patterns, drafting comparison rows — and for production drafting. That's the honest sentence most sites in this niche won't write.

Here is the rest of the sentence. What AI does not do at MysticDo:

- **Decide conclusions.** Recommendations come from the frameworks on this page, applied by a person.
- **Verify facts.** Every price, policy, and claim gets checked by a human against the source before it stays on a page.
- **Publish.** Nothing goes live without human review — specifically on factual accuracy, affiliate compliance, provider claims, anything touching grief or crisis, and final sign-off.

If AI assists a page and we later find an error, that's *our* error, not the tool's. Accountability doesn't delegate.

## Affiliate disclosure & editorial independence

Some links on MysticDo are affiliate links. If you sign up for a service through one of them, we may earn a commission at no additional cost to you. This is currently the site's primary revenue model — we're not going to describe a fantasy version of this site where money isn't involved.

The more interesting question is what the money cannot buy:

- **Ranking.** Providers are not ranked by commission size. (We publish no overall rankings at all — see [why](#no-scores).)
- **Inclusion.** A provider is not recommended because it pays more. If it appears, it earned its place under the template.
- **Methodology.** The same template, the same evidence levels, and the same limitations requirement apply to affiliate and non-affiliate providers alike.
- **"Free is enough" calls.** When the right answer costs nothing, we say so — even when a paid affiliate option exists. You'll find this pattern throughout the [guides](https://mysticdo.com/guides/).

Two further commitments. If a provider stops offering affiliate terms, it stays on the site if it remains a legitimate option for users. If a provider changes its terms in ways that harm users, it is removed — regardless of what it pays.

And one structural rule about placement: **an affiliate link is the logical endpoint of a page, never its beginning.** The sequence is problem → judgment → comparison → match → *then* the link. If you ever find a MysticDo page whose reasoning exists to justify a button, that page is broken — tell us and it gets fixed or pulled.

## What we don't do

- Claim any spiritual practice is real or fake.
- Guarantee outcomes — theirs or ours.
- Publish overall provider scores. Dimensions, not verdicts.
- Sell rankings, placements, or links. (If that ever changes, sponsored content will be labeled in plain language, on the page, before you read it.)
- Publish fabricated testimonials or invented user stories.
- Present platform marketing as independent research.
- Treat user reviews as proof of anything except what users report.
- Recommend a paid service where free is genuinely enough.
- Replace licensed medical, legal, financial, or therapeutic advice — see the disclaimers on every relevant page.

One note on what absence means: **if a provider or reader isn't on this site, that's not a verdict.** It usually means we haven't researched it yet. We don't publish hit pieces, and we don't run a blacklist — we'd rather teach the pattern than shout the name, which is why our safety content focuses on red flags you can check yourself.

## Limitations

Intellectual honesty requires separating what will always limit this methodology from what merely limits it today.

### Structural — these don't go away

- **We evaluate services and decision-fit, not the truth of spiritual claims.** No methodology settles that question, and any site claiming otherwise is selling certainty it doesn't have.
- **Spiritual services are irreducibly subjective.** A reader who gives one person genuine clarity will do nothing for the next. No framework, including ours, can predict your experience — only improve your odds of choosing well.
- **Community signals are noisy.** Review platforms can be gamed, and forums over-represent extreme experiences. We weigh patterns, not anecdotes — and patterns can still be wrong.
- **Everything is a snapshot.** Prices, policies, and reader rosters change. There is always lag between a change and our verification of it.

### Current — on the record

- **Provider reviews are in progress.** None are published yet; the standard they must meet is above.
- **The quiz is rule-based**, not a trained model, and it doesn't learn from results yet.
- **Dating is real from September 2026 forward.** Earlier drafts carried illustrative dates; every page now shows an actual revision date.

These limitations aren't legal hedging. They're the honest boundaries of what a small, independent operation can credibly claim — and respecting them is what separates a methodology from a marketing page.

## How and when we update

A static guide becomes a misleading guide. Content in this niche has a short shelf life — prices move, policies change, readers come and go. Update commitments by content type:

| Content type | Cadence | Triggers an immediate update |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Provider pricing & offers | Rechecked on every page revision | Verified price change, new or expired promotion |
| Provider features & policies | Quarterly | Refund policy change, ownership change, verified safety issue |
| Decision guides | Every 6 months | Underlying facts change, error report, new service format |
| Comparisons | Every 6 months | New major provider, format shift (e.g., AI readings), pricing change |
| Quiz logic | When evidence says it's wrong | Consistent pattern of mismatched results |
| This page | Whenever methodology changes | Any change to evidence levels, language rules, AI policy, or disclosure |

From this page forward, revised pages carry real revision dates. A recommendation can move down or disappear — positions here are not sold, and not permanent.

## Corrections

If you find a factual error — a wrong price, a dead link, a misattributed policy — [tell us](https://mysticdo.com/contact). The policy is simple:

- **Factual errors** are corrected within 72 hours of verification, with the correction noted where space allows.
- **Methodology changes** are never silent — they're documented in the changelog below with the date.
- **Disagreements with our judgment calls** aren't errors; that's what the Level 4 label is for. You can discount our judgment with full information, which is more than most sites offer.
